claims.summary: The SDK unit says the root client owns connection pools and routing caches, so retaining that object targets repeated connection setup. This does not guarantee that subsequent query execution is fast.
The query unit documents projection for reducing response payload. That is useful when data transfer is the bottleneck, but it does not retain the client-owned connections identified here.
The query unit documents page-size control for per-page memory and round-trip tradeoffs. It is a genuine paging option, not a way to retain a newly discarded root client pool.

sourceReviews.supportingSummary: Client entry point and best-practices sections explicitly assign connections/routing cache to CosmosClient, recommend application lifetime, and distinguish lightweight handles from read_item and query operations. Do not adopt the overbroad account-key privileges, conditional-access language or incorrect if_match example.

Read SELECT/projection, WHERE, @name/value arrays, explicit partition_key, max_item_count and iterator execution sections. These establish value binding, eligibility versus shape, and paging; no fixed RU saving, automatic global query-plan cache or universal continuation guarantee is inferred.

choiceReviews.rationale: The SDK connection-best-practices section assigns pooling and routing caches to CosmosClient and explicitly recommends startup/application scope. This addresses the measured setup delay; a per-request client is reasonable only for separately bounded application lifetimes, not this repeated same-account path.
Projection reduces returned fields and response transfer, so it is useful for a payload bottleneck. It leaves the root-client creation that profiling identifies untouched.
max_item_count trades page memory against round trips after query execution begins. It is useful for oversized result pages, not retaining a pool discarded before each request.
